option_description: Controls whether the container runs in privileged mode, which grants the full set of host Linux capabilities, bypasses AppArmor/SELinux LSM enforcement, disables seccomp filtering, and removes most kernel namespace isolation primitives including device restrictions.
security_impact: Privileged mode is the single most critical container misconfiguration. The Rego policy fires `excessive_linux_capabilities_granted` and `privileged_container_flag_dissolving_boundary` directly when `privileged_mode_enabled == true`, triggering two separate high-criticality (score 8) exposures. A privileged container collapses the container trust boundary entirely, enabling direct host escape (T1611), host filesystem access, and nullification of all other security controls including LSM and seccomp profiles that are independently assessed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect a running container's privilege state using docker inspect, filtering for the Privileged field in HostConfig.
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect --format='{{.HostConfig.Privileged}}' <container_id_or_name>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'true' indicates privileged mode is active; 'false' is the expected safe value.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Audit all running containers on a host for privileged mode in a single pass, outputting container name alongside privilege status.
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect $(docker ps -q) --format='{{.Name}}: {{.HostConfig.Privileged}}' 2>/dev/null | grep -i true
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any output lines indicate privileged containers that require remediation. No output means no privileged containers detected.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Kubernetes pod specs across all namespaces for containers with securityContext.privileged set to true using kubectl.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name + ": " + (.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged // false | tostring)' | grep true
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing namespace/pod-name: true indicate privileged containers. No output is the secure state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Kubernetes pod or deployment manifest YAML directly for the privileged flag within each container's securityContext block.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Look for 'privileged: true' under spec.containers[].securityContext. Absence of the field or 'privileged: false' is correct.

typical_values: true (misconfigured — common in legacy infrastructure, DaemonSets requiring device access, and debug workloads)

option_description: Enumerates the list of high-risk Linux capabilities explicitly added to the container's effective capability set beyond the default minimal set. High-risk capabilities include CAP_NET_ADMIN (network stack manipulation), CAP_SYS_PTRACE (cross-process inspection), CAP_SYS_MODULE (kernel module loading), CAP_SYS_ADMIN (broad host administration), and CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE (bypass file permission checks).
security_impact: The Rego rule `excessive_linux_capabilities_granted` fires when `count(input.dangerous_capabilities_granted) > 0`, generating a high-criticality (score 8) exposure. Each listed capability represents a specific attack vector: CAP_SYS_PTRACE enables T1055.008 process injection across zone boundaries; CAP_SYS_MODULE enables T1547.006 kernel module loading for persistent host compromise; CAP_SYS_ADMIN is functionally equivalent to privileged mode and enables container escape (T1611). These capabilities dissolve specific trust boundary enforcement points even without full privileged mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the effective capability set of a running container process by reading from /proc within the container or using capsh on the host.
how_to_obtain.command: docker exec <container_id> cat /proc/1/status | grep -E '^Cap(Inh|Prm|Eff|Bnd|Amb):'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Hex capability masks. Decode with 'capsh --decode=<hex_value>' to see capability names. Look for SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, SYS_MODULE, DAC_OVERRIDE.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Decode capability hex values obtained from /proc/1/status to human-readable names using capsh.
how_to_obtain.command: docker exec <container_id> sh -c 'cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff' | awk '{print $2}' | xargs -I{} capsh --decode={}
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Comma-separated list of active capabilities. Any of cap_sys_admin, cap_net_admin, cap_sys_ptrace, cap_sys_module, cap_dac_override indicate dangerous grants.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query Kubernetes pod specifications for capabilities added via securityContext.capabilities.add across all namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name as $pod | .spec.containers[] | $pod + "/" + .name + ": " + ((.securityContext.capabilities.add // []) | join(","))' | grep -v ':$'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing pod and container names with their added capabilities. Any entry containing SYS_ADMIN, NET_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, SYS_MODULE, or DAC_OVERRIDE requires investigation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the container runtime OCI spec (config.json) for capabilities fields in the process.capabilities section if using containerd or runc directly.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /run/containerd/io.containerd.runtime.v2.task/default/<container_id>/config.json | jq '.process.capabilities'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON object with bounding, effective, inheritable, permitted, and ambient capability arrays. High-risk capability strings in any array indicate misconfiguration.

typical_values: ["SYS_ADMIN"] (high-risk — found in storage drivers and legacy applications)
["SYS_PTRACE"] (found in debugging and APM agent containers)

option_description: Indicates whether the container security configuration explicitly drops ALL Linux capabilities as a baseline before selectively adding back only those strictly required. In Kubernetes this is expressed as capabilities.drop: [ALL] in the container securityContext. This is the recommended hardening baseline per CIS Kubernetes Benchmark and NSA/CISA guidance.
security_impact: The Rego rule `excessive_linux_capabilities_granted` fires when `not input.all_capabilities_dropped` AND `count(input.dropped_capabilities) == 0` AND `not input.privileged_mode_enabled`, meaning a container that neither drops all capabilities nor explicitly drops individual ones nor is privileged still triggers a high-criticality exposure. Setting all_capabilities_dropped to true is the foundational defense: it removes the default capability set (which includes CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, CAP_CHOWN, CAP_SETUID, CAP_SETGID and others) that can be abused for privilege escalation within the container and toward the host.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Kubernetes pod specifications for capabilities.drop: [ALL] in the container securityContext using kubectl across all namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name as $pod | .spec.containers[] | $pod + "/" + .name + ": drop=" + ((.securityContext.capabilities.drop // []) | join(","))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing 'drop=ALL' indicate compliant containers. Lines showing 'drop=' with empty or partial lists indicate missing baseline capability drop.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use kubectl to specifically identify pods missing the 'ALL' capability drop, indicating the baseline hardening is not applied.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities.drop | . == null or (map(ascii_upcase) | contains(["ALL"]) | not)) | .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any listed pod names indicate workloads lacking the drop-all baseline. No output means all pods have the ALL drop applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect deployment or pod manifest YAML files directly for the capabilities.drop field in the container securityContext section.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'capabilities' /path/to/manifests/ | grep -A5 'drop'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: YAML showing '- ALL' under the drop list is compliant. Absence of the drop field or partial lists indicate the baseline is not enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server directly to inspect security contexts for running pods in a specific namespace.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl get secret -n kube-system default-token -o jsonpath={.data.token} | base64 -d)' https://<api-server>:6443/api/v1/namespaces/<namespace>/pods | jq -r '.items[].spec.containers[].securityContext.capabilities.drop'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Arrays containing 'ALL' for each container indicate compliant configurations. null or empty arrays require remediation.

typical_values: false (default — capabilities are not dropped, common in unmodified deployments)
true (hardened deployments following CIS benchmarks or PodSecurityPolicy/PodSecurityAdmission enforcement)

option_description: Contains the explicit list of individual Linux capabilities dropped from the container's capability set via securityContext.capabilities.drop in Kubernetes or equivalent runtime configuration. Unlike all_capabilities_dropped which is a binary baseline, this attribute records granular per-capability drops when the drop-all approach is not used, allowing partial hardening assessment.
security_impact: The Rego rule `excessive_linux_capabilities_granted` evaluates `count(input.dropped_capabilities) == 0` as a condition alongside `not input.all_capabilities_dropped` to detect containers with no capability reduction at all. An empty dropped_capabilities list combined with all_capabilities_dropped=false means the container retains the full default capability set, which includes capabilities enabling privilege escalation and boundary violations. This attribute provides granular evidence for determining whether specific high-risk capabilities (CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, CAP_SYS_MODULE) have been individually removed when a drop-all approach is not feasible.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract the explicitly dropped capabilities list for all containers across all Kubernetes namespaces, showing the drop configuration per container.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name as $pod | .spec.containers[] | $pod + "/" + .name + ": " + ((.securityContext.capabilities.drop // []) | join(", "))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing capability names in the drop list. Empty values after the colon indicate no capabilities are dropped, which is a finding requiring remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the effective bounding capability set of a running container to confirm drops have been applied at the kernel level, not just specified in config.
how_to_obtain.command: docker exec <container_id> sh -c 'capsh --print | grep Bounding'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The bounding set should show a reduced set of capabilities. Full capability set in the bounding set (e.g., '= cap_chown,cap_dac_override,...38 capabilities') indicates no drops have been applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For containerd-managed containers, inspect the OCI runtime spec to see the permitted and effective capability arrays which reflect actual drops.
how_to_obtain.command: ctr -n k8s.io containers info <container_id> | jq '.Spec.process.capabilities'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON showing bounding, effective, permitted, inheritable, and ambient arrays. Shorter arrays compared to full Linux capability list indicate successful drops.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Audit Kubernetes manifest files in a repository or on disk for the capabilities.drop field to identify what individual capabilities are being dropped.
how_to_obtain.command: find /path/to/manifests -name '*.yaml' -exec grep -l 'capabilities' {} \; | xargs -I{} sh -c 'echo "=== {} ==="; grep -A10 capabilities {}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: YAML sections showing drop lists with capability names. Files with no drop section or empty drop lists require remediation.

typical_values: [] (default — no explicit drops, most common in legacy deployments)
["ALL"] (when drop: [ALL] is specified, equivalent to all_capabilities_dropped=true)

option_description: Specifies the type of seccomp (secure computing mode) syscall filtering profile applied to the container. 'Unconfined' permits all syscalls with no filtering. 'RuntimeDefault' applies the container runtime's built-in restrictive profile (e.g., Docker's or containerd's default). 'Localhost' uses a custom seccomp profile file stored on the node. 'None' indicates the seccompProfile field is entirely absent from the pod/container spec.
security_impact: Two Rego conditions directly evaluate this attribute: `missing_or_permissive_seccomp_profile` fires when `seccomp_profile_type == 'Unconfined'` or `seccomp_profile_type == 'None'`, both triggering a high-criticality (score 8) exposure. Without syscall filtering, workloads can invoke ptrace (T1055.008) to inspect and inject into cross-zone processes, mount syscalls to access host filesystems, keyctl to steal kernel keyrings, and init_module/finit_module for kernel module loading (T1547.006), all of which constitute direct trust boundary bypass paths. RuntimeDefault blocks approximately 44+ dangerous syscalls and is the minimum acceptable configuration; Localhost with a custom profile is required for workloads needing tighter or modified controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query all Kubernetes pods for their seccomp profile type at both pod and container level, checking both the modern seccompProfile field and legacy annotations.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name + ": podLevel=" + (.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type // "None") + " annotation=" + (.metadata.annotations["seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod"] // "absent")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing 'RuntimeDefault' or 'Localhost' at pod level indicate configured filtering. 'None' or 'Unconfined' values require remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check container-level seccomp profile type overrides which take precedence over pod-level configuration in Kubernetes.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name as $pod | .spec.containers[] | $pod + "/" + .name + ": " + (.securityContext.seccompProfile.type // "None")'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Per-container seccomp type values. 'None' means the container inherits pod-level setting or has no profile if pod level is also absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Docker containers, inspect the seccomp profile applied via docker inspect examining the SecurityOpt field.
how_to_obtain.command:
docker inspect <container_id> --format='{{range .HostConfig.SecurityOpt}}{{.}}
{{end}}' | grep seccomp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'seccomp=unconfined' indicates no filtering. 'seccomp={...json...}' or a profile path indicates filtering is active. Absence of seccomp line means runtime default may or may not apply depending on daemon configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify the effective seccomp filter on a running process by examining /proc/[pid]/status for the Seccomp field inside the container.
how_to_obtain.command: docker exec <container_id> cat /proc/1/status | grep Seccomp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Seccomp: 0' means unconfined (no filter). 'Seccomp: 1' means strict mode. 'Seccomp: 2' means filter mode (seccomp-bpf active, which is the desired state for RuntimeDefault or Localhost profiles).

typical_values: None (most common in unmodified Kubernetes deployments prior to v1.27)
RuntimeDefault (hardened deployments, required by default in Kubernetes 1.27+ PodSecurityAdmission restricted profile)
Unconfined (explicitly disabled — found in legacy or debug workloads)
Localhost (specialized workloads with custom syscall requirements)

option_description: A boolean indicator of whether any seccomp profile is explicitly configured on the pod or container security context, including both the modern Kubernetes seccompProfile field (v1.19+) and legacy seccomp annotations. False indicates the seccomp configuration is entirely absent, which defaults to unconfined behavior in most runtimes including Docker and containerd without daemon-level defaults.
security_impact: The Rego rule `missing_or_permissive_seccomp_profile` fires on `not input.seccomp_profile_configured`, producing a high-criticality (score 8) exposure even when seccomp_profile_type is not explicitly set to Unconfined — absence itself is treated as permissive. This matters because Kubernetes before 1.27 does not apply any seccomp profile by default, meaning the vast majority of production workloads silently run unconfined. Without explicit configuration, the syscall surface is fully exposed, enabling namespace escape primitives, process tracing across zone boundaries, and kernel module loading, all of which bypass container trust boundary enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify all pods with no seccomp configuration by checking both modern seccompProfile fields and legacy annotations simultaneously.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select((.spec.securityContext.seccompProfile == null) and (.metadata.annotations["seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod"] == null) and (.spec.containers[].securityContext.seccompProfile == null)) | .metadata.namespace + "/" + .metadata.name'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any listed pods have no seccomp profile configured and are running unconfined. No output indicates all pods have some seccomp configuration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the container runtime daemon has a global seccomp default configured, which would apply when pod-level configuration is absent.
how_to_obtain.command:
docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}' | tr ',' '
' | grep seccomp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'name=seccomp,profile=default' indicates the Docker daemon applies its default seccomp profile when not explicitly configured. Absence means containers run unconfined if no profile is specified.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For containerd, check the daemon configuration for a default seccomp profile path or unconfined setting.
how_to_obtain.command: containerd config dump | grep -A5 seccomp
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Configuration showing seccomp_profile or sandbox seccomp settings. No seccomp-related configuration means containers rely on pod-level specification only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan Kubernetes manifest files to count and identify those missing seccomp profile configuration entirely.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rL 'seccompProfile\|seccomp.security.alpha' /path/to/manifests/*.yaml | xargs -I{} echo 'Missing seccomp config: {}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files listed as 'Missing seccomp config' require seccompProfile configuration. No output means all manifests have explicit seccomp settings.

typical_values: false (default — dominant in Kubernetes clusters running versions below 1.27 without PodSecurityAdmission restricted enforcement)
true (hardened deployments, clusters with PodSecurityAdmission restricted profile, or explicit seccomp policy enforcement via OPA/Kyverno)

option_description: Indicates whether a Linux Security Module mandatory access control profile (AppArmor, SELinux, or equivalent) is actively applied and enforced on the container at runtime. This is distinct from a profile being merely loaded or present — it requires the profile to be in enforce mode and actually constraining the container process. False means either no LSM profile exists for the container or the profile is in a non-enforcing state.
security_impact: The Rego rule `absent_or_weak_lsm_enforcement` fires on `not input.lsm_profile_enforced`, producing a high-criticality (score 8) exposure. LSM enforcement provides the mandatory access control layer that complements discretionary access controls — it prevents capability misuse from resulting in file system traversal, process manipulation, or network operations outside the container's defined trust zone. The rule also fires when `lsm_profile_enforced == true` but `lsm_profile_mode` is permissive/disabled/unknown, recognizing that a profile that only logs violations (AppArmor complain mode, SELinux permissive) provides no actual enforcement. Without LSM, privileged container exploits and capability abuse (T1611, T1543.005) lack a secondary enforcement layer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check AppArmor enforcement status for container processes by listing enforced profiles via aa-status on the host node.
how_to_obtain.command: aa-status --json 2>/dev/null | jq '.processes | to_entries[] | select(.value[].status == "enforce") | .key + ": " + .value[].profile'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Entries showing container process PIDs with their AppArmor profile name in enforce mode. Processes in 'complain' mode or unlisted indicate absence of enforcement.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify AppArmor profile assignment for a specific Docker container, checking the annotation in docker inspect output.
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect <container_id> --format='AppArmorProfile: {{.AppArmorProfile}}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'AppArmorProfile: docker-default' or a custom profile name indicates enforcement. Empty string means no AppArmor profile is assigned to the container.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check SELinux enforcement state on the host and verify container processes have SELinux labels assigned when SELinux is the active LSM.
how_to_obtain.command: getenforce && ps -eZ | grep <container_process_name>
how_to_obtain.expected_output: First command returns 'Enforcing' (active enforcement), 'Permissive' (logging only), or 'Disabled'. Second command shows the SELinux context label for the container process. A label like 'container_t' or a specific confined type indicates LSM is applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Kubernetes pods, check the AppArmor annotation that controls which profile is loaded for each container in the pod.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod <pod_name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}' | jq 'to_entries[] | select(.key | startswith("container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io")) | .key + "=" + .value'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Annotations showing 'runtime/default' or 'localhost/profile-name' indicate AppArmor is configured. 'unconfined' or absent annotations mean no LSM enforcement for those containers.

typical_values: true (Docker environments — Docker daemon applies docker-default AppArmor profile automatically)
false (containerd/Kubernetes without explicit AppArmor annotation — no automatic profile application)
false (SELinux disabled or in permissive mode on the node)
true (OpenShift with SELinux — SELinux enforce mode is standard)

option_description: Describes the operational mode of the LSM (Linux Security Module) profile applied to the container: 'enforce' mode actively blocks policy violations and prevents disallowed operations; 'permissive' mode logs violations without blocking, providing visibility but no enforcement; 'disabled' means no LSM profile is active for the container; 'unknown' indicates the mode cannot be determined from available information.
security_impact: The Rego rule `absent_or_weak_lsm_enforcement` includes a condition that fires even when `lsm_profile_enforced == true` if `lsm_profile_mode in ['permissive', 'disabled', 'unknown']`. This reflects the security reality that permissive mode (AppArmor complain, SELinux permissive) provides zero actual protection — it only generates audit logs while allowing all operations including those that would constitute boundary violations. The high-criticality (score 8) exposure recognizes that an organization believing LSM is protecting their containers while running in permissive mode has a false security assumption. Only 'enforce' mode constitutes actual mandatory access control that prevents capability abuse (T1611), filesystem traversal, and container service manipulation (T1543.005).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Determine the operational mode of AppArmor profiles for all container processes on the host, distinguishing between enforce and complain modes.
how_to_obtain.command: aa-status 2>/dev/null | grep -E '(enforce|complain)' | head -50
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Sections listing profiles and processes in 'enforce mode' and 'complain mode'. Container processes appearing under 'complain mode' indicate permissive LSM enforcement, which is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For SELinux environments, check the global enforcement mode on the node which applies to all container processes.
how_to_obtain.command: getenforce && sestatus | grep -E '(SELinux status|Current mode|Mode from config)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: getenforce returns 'Enforcing', 'Permissive', or 'Disabled'. sestatus provides additional detail. Only 'Enforcing' represents active LSM protection for containers on this node.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check AppArmor mode for a specific container process by finding its PID and checking its profile status in the aa-status JSON output.
how_to_obtain.command: CPID=$(docker inspect <container_id> --format '{{.State.Pid}}') && aa-status --json | jq --arg pid "$CPID" '.processes[$pid][0] // {status: "unconfined"}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON object with 'status' field. 'enforce' is the secure state. 'complain' means permissive logging only. Absence from aa-status output or 'unconfined' means no LSM profile applied.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On SELinux systems, check the persistent SELinux configuration file to determine the configured mode, which may differ from the current runtime mode after manual changes.
how_to_obtain.command: cat /etc/selinux/config | grep '^SELINUX='
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'SELINUX=enforcing' is the secure configuration. 'SELINUX=permissive' means logs only without blocking. 'SELINUX=disabled' means LSM is entirely inactive on this node for all containers.

typical_values: enforce (Docker with AppArmor on Ubuntu/Debian — docker-default profile in enforce mode)
enforce (OpenShift and RHEL-based Kubernetes with SELinux enforcing)
permissive (SELinux in permissive mode — common on nodes where operators disabled enforcement to troubleshoot and never re-enabled)
disabled (nodes where AppArmor or SELinux was disabled for compatibility reasons)
unknown (mixed environments or when LSM framework is present but profile assignment cannot be verified)

option_description: Controls whether a container or pod is configured to share the host's PID namespace or another container's PID namespace via hostPID: true or shareProcessNamespace: true. When enabled, all processes across the sharing scope become visible and addressable from within the container, breaking process-level isolation.
security_impact: The Rego rule shared_pid_or_ipc_namespace_across_zones fires when shared_pid_namespace == true AND cross_zone_namespace_sharing_detected == true. Shared PID namespaces enable ptrace-based process injection (T1055.008) across workloads in different trust zones, allow /proc filesystem inspection of cross-zone processes, and facilitate escape to host (T1611) by interacting with privileged host processes. Even without cross-zone sharing, enabling hostPID exposes all host processes to the container.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query all pod specs in a Kubernetes namespace for hostPID and shareProcessNamespace fields using kubectl
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, hostPID: .spec.hostPID, shareProcessNamespace: .spec.shareProcessNamespace}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects per pod; hostPID or shareProcessNamespace fields present and set to true indicate the configuration is enabled. Absence or false values indicate safe state.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect a specific pod spec directly for PID namespace sharing fields
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.hostPID}{" "}{.spec.shareProcessNamespace}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'true true', 'true false', 'false true', or 'false false'. Any true value flags the attribute.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the pod or deployment manifest YAML for hostPID and shareProcessNamespace fields under spec
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Under spec: hostPID: true or shareProcessNamespace: true indicates shared PID namespace is enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Docker or containerd workloads, inspect the container's PID mode using docker inspect
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect <container-id> --format '{{.HostConfig.PidMode}}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'host' indicates hostPID sharing. Output of 'container:<name>' indicates sharing with another container. Empty output indicates isolated PID namespace (safe).

option_description: Controls whether a container is configured to share the host's IPC namespace via hostIPC: true or another container's IPC namespace via --ipc=container. When enabled, shared memory segments, semaphores, and POSIX message queues become accessible across the sharing boundary, allowing cross-container or cross-host IPC communication.
security_impact: The Rego rule shared_pid_or_ipc_namespace_across_zones fires when shared_ipc_namespace == true AND cross_zone_namespace_sharing_detected == true. Shared IPC namespaces enable inter-process communication abuse (T1559), allowing a compromised container to read or write shared memory segments belonging to processes in other trust zones. Combined with cross-zone sharing, this constitutes a direct segmentation enforcement failure enabling lateral movement and potential escape to host (T1611).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query all pod specs across namespaces for hostIPC configuration using kubectl
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostIPC == true) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, hostIPC: .spec.hostIPC}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any returned objects indicate pods with hostIPC: true enabled. Empty output means no pods have shared IPC namespace.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check a specific pod's IPC namespace configuration
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.hostIPC}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'true' indicates shared IPC namespace is enabled. Empty or 'false' indicates isolated IPC namespace.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Docker workloads, inspect the IPC mode of a running container
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect <container-id> --format '{{.HostConfig.IpcMode}}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'host' indicates host IPC namespace sharing. Output of 'container:<name>' indicates sharing with a specific container. Output of 'private' or 'shareable' indicates safe isolation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search pod and deployment manifest files for hostIPC field
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'hostIPC' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ /path/to/helm/charts/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines matching 'hostIPC: true' indicate the misconfiguration. No output or 'hostIPC: false' indicates safe configuration.

option_description: A derived analytical determination indicating whether PID or IPC namespace sharing has been confirmed between containers belonging to different trust zones. This requires correlating namespace-sharing configuration (hostPID, hostIPC, shareProcessNamespace, --pid=container, --ipc=container) with trust zone labels assigned to each container. True only when two or more co-sharing containers carry distinct trust zone labels.
security_impact: This attribute is the critical co-condition in the Rego rule shared_pid_or_ipc_namespace_across_zones. The rule fires only when (shared_pid_namespace OR shared_ipc_namespace) == true AND cross_zone_namespace_sharing_detected == true. Without confirmed cross-zone sharing, namespace sharing within the same zone may be acceptable. With it, the exposure represents a direct namespace-level segmentation breach enabling ptrace injection (T1055.008), IPC abuse (T1559), and escape to host (T1611) across zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify all pods sharing PID or IPC namespaces and retrieve their trust-zone labels for cross-zone correlation
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '[.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, zone: .metadata.labels["trust-zone"], hostPID: .spec.hostPID, hostIPC: .spec.hostIPC, shareProcessNamespace: .spec.shareProcessNamespace}] | group_by(.namespace)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Grouped pod objects showing zone labels alongside namespace-sharing flags. Flag as true if any co-sharing pods within the same pod (shareProcessNamespace) or on the same host (hostPID/hostIPC) have different trust-zone label values.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Find pods that share namespaces with containers in different namespaces or node pools and compare zone label annotations
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.shareProcessNamespace == true or .spec.hostPID == true or .spec.hostIPC == true) | {name: .metadata.name, ns: .metadata.namespace, labels: .metadata.labels}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of pods with namespace sharing enabled; manually or programmatically compare 'trust-zone' or equivalent label values across pods sharing the same node or pod spec.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the cluster's trust zone label taxonomy with platform engineers to confirm which label keys (e.g., trust-zone, security-tier, environment) denote zone boundaries, then re-run namespace-sharing queries filtered against those labels
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A confirmed label key and value set representing each trust zone (e.g., trust-zone=dmz, trust-zone=internal), enabling accurate cross-zone correlation queries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes API to retrieve pod specs and labels for cross-zone namespace sharing analysis
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://<api-server>/api/v1/pods | jq '[.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, zoneLabel: .metadata.labels["trust-zone"], hostPID: .spec.hostPID, hostIPC: .spec.hostIPC}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of pods with zone labels and sharing flags. Cross-zone sharing is confirmed when two entries with different zoneLabel values share the same pod spec or are co-located on the same node with host-level sharing.

option_description: Indicates whether a CNI-level NetworkPolicy resource with egress rules—or an equivalent egress filtering mechanism—is applied to the workload's pod selector, restricting outbound connections to only explicitly permitted destinations. This requires both the existence of an egress policy and a CNI plugin that enforces it (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Weave, Antrea).
security_impact: The Rego rule unrestricted_egress_enabling_trust_propagation fires when egress_network_policy_enforced is false AND (workload_trust_zone is 'untrusted' or 'low') OR when cloud_metadata_service_reachable is true AND egress_network_policy_enforced is false. Without egress policies, containers can initiate outbound connections to higher-trust zones (T1590.003), bridge network boundaries (T1599), exfiltrate data to external C2, or reach the cloud metadata service for credential theft.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all NetworkPolicy resources in a namespace and inspect their egress rules
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace> -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, podSelector: .spec.podSelector, egress: .spec.egress, policyTypes: .spec.policyTypes}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: NetworkPolicy objects should contain 'Egress' in policyTypes and a non-empty egress array. If no NetworkPolicy exists, or none include Egress in policyTypes, egress is unenforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether the CNI plugin in use supports and is configured to enforce egress NetworkPolicy
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave|antrea|flannel'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of Calico, Cilium, Antrea, or Weave confirms egress policy enforcement capability. Flannel alone does not enforce NetworkPolicy and requires a separate network policy controller.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify whether a specific workload's pod selector is matched by any NetworkPolicy with egress rules
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace> -o json | jq --arg label 'app=<workload>' '.items[] | select(.spec.policyTypes[] == "Egress") | select(.spec.podSelector.matchLabels | to_entries[] | .key + "=" + .value == $label)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more NetworkPolicy objects matching the workload selector with Egress in policyTypes confirms egress enforcement. No match means no egress policy covers this workload.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API for NetworkPolicy resources targeting the workload namespace and confirm egress rule presence
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://<api-server>/apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/<namespace>/networkpolicies | jq '[.items[] | select(.spec.policyTypes[] == "Egress") | {name: .metadata.name, egress: .spec.egress}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of NetworkPolicy objects with non-null egress arrays confirms egress policies exist. Empty array means no egress policies are defined.

option_description: Indicates whether a container can successfully reach the cloud instance metadata service (IMDS) at 169.254.169.254 (or equivalent provider endpoints such as fd00:ec2::254 for AWS IPv6, or metadata.google.internal for GCP). This is determined by attempting a connection from within the container and verifying no egress NetworkPolicy explicitly denies this CIDR/destination.
security_impact: The Rego rule unrestricted_egress_enabling_trust_propagation fires when cloud_metadata_service_reachable == true AND egress_network_policy_enforced is false. Reachability of the metadata service allows any process in the container to request instance identity credentials, IAM role tokens, or user-data secrets associated with the underlying node (T1552, T1590.003). This enables credential theft that can be used to pivot to higher-trust cloud resources, bridging network zone boundaries (T1599).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Execute a connectivity test from within the target container to the IMDS endpoint to verify reachability
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <namespace> <pod-name> -c <container-name> -- curl -s --connect-timeout 3 http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A successful HTTP response (e.g., listing of metadata keys like 'ami-id', 'instance-id') confirms the metadata service is reachable. A connection timeout or refused connection indicates it is blocked.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect NetworkPolicy egress rules for explicit deny or absence of allow rules covering 169.254.169.254/32
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace> -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.policyTypes[] == "Egress") | .spec.egress[] | select(.to[]?.ipBlock?.cidr) | .to[].ipBlock'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: CIDR entries should include an explicit block for 169.254.169.254/32 or absence of any allow rule covering that IP. If no egress policy at all exists, treat metadata service as reachable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test metadata service reachability using wget with a short timeout from a debug container on the same node
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl run metadata-test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n <namespace> -- wget -q -T 3 -O - http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ 2>&1
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Successful output of metadata keys confirms reachability. 'wget: server returned error: HTTP/1.0 401' still confirms network path is open. Connection timeout confirms blocking.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for Cilium or Calico egress rules specifically blocking the link-local metadata CIDR
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get ciliumnetworkpolicies -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.egress[]?.toCIDRSet[]?.cidr == "169.254.169.254/32")' 2>/dev/null || kubectl get globalnetworkpolicies.crd.projectcalico.org -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.egress[]?.destination?.nets[] | contains("169.254.169.254"))' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Matching policy objects with a deny action or absence from allow rules for 169.254.169.254/32 confirms the IMDS is blocked. No match means the path may be open.

option_description: Enumerates the broadest effective scope of ingress network policy rules applied to a workload or namespace. 'none' means no NetworkPolicy restricts ingress (fully open). 'namespace_wide' means a policy uses an empty podSelector matching all pods within the namespace. 'cluster_wide' means namespaceSelector: {} or equivalent matches all namespaces. 'zone_scoped' means selectors reference specific trust-zone labels, enforcing zone-boundary-aware restrictions.
security_impact: The Rego rule overly_permissive_ingress_between_zones fires when ingress_policy_scope is 'none' AND cross_zone_ingress_enforced is false, OR when ingress_policy_scope is 'cluster_wide' AND cross_zone_ingress_enforced is false, OR when default_deny_ingress_policy_present is false AND cross_zone_ingress_enforced is false AND scope is not 'zone_scoped'. Broad ingress scopes create lateral movement paths (T1599) by allowing attackers in low-trust zones to directly address services in higher-trust zones without traversing any enforcement point, exploiting implicit network trust dependencies (T1590.003).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Retrieve all NetworkPolicy resources in a namespace and analyze the broadest ingress selector scope
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace> -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.policyTypes[] == "Ingress" or (.spec.ingress | length > 0)) | {name: .metadata.name, podSelector: .spec.podSelector, ingressFrom: [.spec.ingress[]?.from[]?]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Examine podSelector and ingressFrom fields: empty podSelector ({}) means policy applies to all pods; namespaceSelector:{} in from rules means cluster-wide ingress allowed; absence of NetworkPolicy means scope is 'none'; zone-label selectors indicate 'zone_scoped'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for cluster-wide ingress exposure by finding policies with unrestricted namespaceSelector
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.ingress[]?.from[]?.namespaceSelector == {}) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, scope: "cluster_wide"}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any returned objects indicate NetworkPolicy rules with unrestricted namespaceSelector, confirming cluster_wide ingress scope. Empty output means no cluster-wide ingress policies exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Determine if any NetworkPolicy exists at all in the namespace; absence implies scope of 'none'
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace> 2>&1
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'No resources found' confirms ingress_policy_scope is 'none'. Presence of policies requires further inspection to determine scope level.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes API to retrieve and analyze ingress NetworkPolicy scopes across all namespaces
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://<api-server>/apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/networkpolicies | jq '[.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, policyTypes: .spec.policyTypes, ingressFrom: [.spec.ingress[]?.from[]?]}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Array of policies with ingress from-selectors; evaluate each from clause: absence=none, empty namespaceSelector=cluster_wide, empty podSelector=namespace_wide, labeled selectors=zone_scoped.

option_description: Indicates whether NetworkPolicy ingress rules explicitly reference trust-zone-identifying labels on namespaceSelector or podSelector fields, thereby restricting ingress to only containers carrying approved zone labels. True only when at least one ingress rule uses a selector that references a recognized zone-identification label key (e.g., trust-zone, security-tier, environment) with a specific zone value.
security_impact: The Rego rule overly_permissive_ingress_between_zones fires in three conditions, all of which require cross_zone_ingress_enforced to be false as a co-condition. Without zone-label-based ingress enforcement, network policies cannot distinguish between traffic originating from different trust zones. This allows attackers in low-trust zones to exploit implicit trust relationships (T1590.003) and bridge zone boundaries (T1599) by directly initiating connections to services that should only accept traffic from specific zones, enabling trust modification abuse (T1484.002).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect NetworkPolicy ingress rules for zone-identifying label selectors on namespaceSelector or podSelector
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace> -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, ingressFrom: [.spec.ingress[]?.from[]? | {namespaceSelector: .namespaceSelector, podSelector: .podSelector}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ingress from-rules should contain namespaceSelector.matchLabels or podSelector.matchLabels referencing a trust-zone label key (e.g., 'trust-zone': 'internal'). Absence of zone-label references in all from-rules means cross_zone_ingress_enforced is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search specifically for NetworkPolicy ingress rules using a known zone label key across all namespaces
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | jq '[.items[] | select(.spec.ingress[]?.from[]? | (.namespaceSelector.matchLabels // .podSelector.matchLabels) | has("trust-zone")) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returned objects confirm zone-label-based ingress enforcement exists. Empty array means no NetworkPolicy ingress rules reference the zone label, confirming cross_zone_ingress_enforced is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview platform or security engineers to confirm the label key used to identify trust zones and verify that label is consistently applied to all namespaces and pods, then re-run selector queries against that label
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documented label key-value pairs for each trust zone (e.g., trust-zone=dmz, trust-zone=internal, trust-zone=restricted) enabling accurate ingress enforcement queries.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that namespace objects carry the expected zone labels which NetworkPolicy selectors reference
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, zoneLabel: .metadata.labels["trust-zone"]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All namespaces should have a trust-zone label populated. Namespaces without zone labels cannot be selected by zone-based NetworkPolicy rules, making cross-zone enforcement effectively impossible regardless of policy content.

option_description: Indicates whether a default-deny NetworkPolicy exists in the namespace that selects all pods (using an empty podSelector: {}) with an Ingress policyType and an empty or absent ingress rules array, effectively blocking all ingress traffic unless explicitly permitted by a separate allow-rule NetworkPolicy. This is the foundational baseline control for namespace-level ingress segmentation.
security_impact: The Rego rule overly_permissive_ingress_between_zones includes a condition where default_deny_ingress_policy_present is false AND cross_zone_ingress_enforced is false AND ingress_policy_scope is not 'zone_scoped'. Without a default-deny baseline, all ingress is implicitly permitted to pods not covered by any NetworkPolicy, creating lateral movement paths (T1599) between trust zones. Attackers in lower-trust zones can directly access services in higher-trust zones by exploiting the absence of a deny baseline, abusing implicit network trust dependencies (T1590.003) and enabling trust modification (T1484.002).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search for a default-deny NetworkPolicy in the target namespace by looking for empty podSelector with Ingress policyType and no ingress rules
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -n <namespace> -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} and (.spec.policyTypes[] == "Ingress") and (.spec.ingress == null or (.spec.ingress | length == 0))) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: One or more matching objects confirm a default-deny ingress policy is present. Empty output means no default-deny policy exists in the namespace.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check all namespaces for presence of default-deny ingress policies to identify gaps across the cluster
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy -A -o json | jq '[.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} and (.spec.policyTypes[]? == "Ingress") and (.spec.ingress == null or (.spec.ingress | length == 0))) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace}] | group_by(.namespace)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Grouped results showing which namespaces have default-deny ingress policies. Namespaces absent from results lack the baseline deny policy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review stored Helm chart values or GitOps manifests for default-deny NetworkPolicy definitions
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'policyTypes' /path/to/manifests/ | grep -i 'ingress' | xargs grep -l 'podSelector: {}' 2>/dev/null
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Files containing both 'podSelector: {}' and 'Ingress' policyType with no ingress rules array confirm default-deny policies are defined in the deployment manifests.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Kubernetes API to programmatically verify default-deny ingress policy presence in a specific namespace
how_to_obtain.command: curl -sk -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' https://<api-server>/apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/<namespace>/networkpolicies | jq '[.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} and (.spec.policyTypes[]? == "Ingress") and (.spec.ingress == null or .spec.ingress == []))]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-empty array confirms default-deny policy exists. Empty array '[]' confirms the policy is absent and the attribute should be set to false.

option_description: Controls whether Kubernetes secrets are projected as environment variables into pods that reside in a different trust zone than the zone owning the secret, or whether init containers carrying embedded secrets are shared across trust zone boundaries. A true value indicates a cross-zone credential boundary violation is present.
security_impact: When true, the Rego rule `environment_variable_credential_bleed_across_zones` fires immediately, triggering the 'Environment Variable Credential Bleed Across Zones' exposure. Secrets accessible via environment variables in cross-zone pods allow a compromised workload in a lower-trust zone to authenticate against higher-trust zone services, collapsing zone separation. The policy checks this attribute directly as a standalone trigger condition.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate all pods with envFrom secretRef blocks and compare the owning namespace trust zone label against the pod's namespace trust zone label to detect cross-zone projection.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].envFrom[]?.secretRef != null) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, (.spec.containers[].envFrom[]?.secretRef.name // empty)] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Tab-separated list of namespace, pod name, and secret name; cross-reference namespace trust zone labels to identify boundary violations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify init containers referencing secrets across namespace boundaries using env secretKeyRef inspection.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.initContainers != null) | .metadata.namespace as $ns | .metadata.name as $pod | .spec.initContainers[].env[]? | select(.valueFrom.secretKeyRef != null) | [$ns, $pod, .name, .valueFrom.secretKeyRef.name] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of init containers referencing secrets; verify the owning secret's namespace trust-zone annotation differs from the pod's namespace.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check RBAC policies to identify if service accounts in one trust zone namespace are granted get/list access to secrets in another zone's namespace.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.roleRef.kind == "ClusterRole" or .roleRef.kind == "Role") | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, (.subjects[]?.namespace // "cluster")] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Bindings where subjects from a different namespace (zone) than the binding namespace have access to secret resources.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API for projected volume sources of type secret across all pods and filter by zone-labeled namespace mismatches.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '[.items[] | {ns: .metadata.namespace, pod: .metadata.name, projected_secrets: [.spec.volumes[]? | select(.projected != null) | .projected.sources[]? | select(.secret != null) | .secret.localObjectReference.name]}] | map(select(.projected_secrets | length > 0))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of pods with projected secret volumes; cross-reference secret namespace ownership against pod namespace trust zone labels.

option_description: Defines the trust zone scope of sidecar injection mechanisms such as service mesh proxies (Istio, Linkerd) or secrets agent sidecars. 'single_zone' means injection is restricted to namespaces within one trust zone; 'multi_zone' means injection spans defined but multiple zones; 'unrestricted' means injection is applied cluster-wide without zone boundary enforcement.
security_impact: When set to 'multi_zone' or 'unrestricted', the Rego rule `environment_variable_credential_bleed_across_zones` fires, generating the credential bleed exposure. Injected sidecars may carry environment variables referencing secrets from their origin zone, and when injected into pods in a different zone they propagate those credentials across the trust boundary. The policy uses an `in` operator checking for these two enum values as standalone triggers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects to determine which namespaceSelector rules govern sidecar injection scope and whether they are restricted to single-zone namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfigurations -o json | jq -r '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, webhooks: [.webhooks[]? | {name: .name, namespaceSelector: .namespaceSelector, objectSelector: .objectSelector}]}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If namespaceSelector uses matchLabels targeting a single trust-zone label, scope is single_zone; absence of zone-scoped selectors indicates multi_zone or unrestricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List namespaces with the sidecar injection enabled annotation and check their trust zone labels to determine injection breadth.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations["istio-injection"] == "enabled" or .metadata.labels["sidecar.istio.io/inject"] == "true") | [.metadata.name, (.metadata.labels["trust-zone"] // "unset")] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Namespaces with injection enabled; if trust-zone label values span multiple distinct zones, scope is multi_zone; if label is absent or set to all zones, scope is unrestricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Istio or Linkerd control plane configuration for injection scope settings in the mesh configuration file.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap -n istio-system istio -o jsonpath='{.data.mesh}' | grep -E 'enableAutoInjection|injectNamespace|namespaceSelector'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of namespace-scoped injection selectors constrained to a single trust-zone label confirms single_zone; broad or absent selectors indicate multi_zone or unrestricted.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform team to determine if sidecar injection policies are documented and enforced via admission control, and whether secret environment variable payloads in sidecars are audited for cross-zone references.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Documentation showing zone-scoped injection namespaceSelectors and evidence that sidecar secret payloads are reviewed for cross-zone credential references.

option_description: Indicates whether a Kubernetes service account token is mounted into a container, either through the default automountServiceAccountToken mechanism or via an explicit projected volume of type ServiceAccountToken. When true, the container has a credential allowing it to authenticate against the Kubernetes API server.
security_impact: When true and combined with missing audience binding (`token_audience_binding_configured` is false) or a long-lived token (`token_long_lived` is true), the Rego rule `service_account_token_over_projection` fires, generating the 'Service Account Token Over Projection' exposure. A token present in a container that is compromised can be extracted and used to authenticate to the API server or adjacent zone services, enabling privilege escalation and trust zone traversal.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check all pods for automountServiceAccountToken set to true or unset (which defaults to true) across all namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.automountServiceAccountToken != false) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, (.spec.automountServiceAccountToken | tostring)] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pods where automountServiceAccountToken is true or null (unset) will appear; absence of the field means token is mounted by default.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Detect explicit projected volumes of type ServiceAccountToken in pod specifications.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.projected.sources[]?.serviceAccountToken != null) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: List of pods with explicit ServiceAccountToken projected volume sources; presence confirms service_account_token_projected is true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify token presence inside a running container by checking the default mount path for the service account token file.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <namespace> <pod-name> -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token 2>/dev/null && echo 'TOKEN_MOUNTED' || echo 'NO_TOKEN'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'TOKEN_MOUNTED' confirms the token is projected into the container filesystem.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check ServiceAccount objects themselves for automountServiceAccountToken setting, as pod-level setting inherits from the ServiceAccount if not overridden.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get serviceaccounts --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.automountServiceAccountToken != false) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Service accounts without automountServiceAccountToken:false will mount tokens into pods by default.

option_description: Indicates whether a projected service account token includes an explicit 'audience' field in its projected volume source, restricting the token's validity to a specific named service audience. When absent, the token is audience-unbound and accepted as valid by any service that trusts the Kubernetes API server's signing key.
security_impact: When false and `service_account_token_projected` is true, the Rego rule `service_account_token_over_projection` fires via the condition `not input.token_audience_binding_configured`. Audience-unbound tokens extracted from a compromised container can authenticate to any Kubernetes API audience or any service using the same OIDC trust chain, enabling cross-zone service impersonation beyond the intended workload scope.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect projected volume sources for serviceAccountToken entries and check whether the audience field is explicitly set.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace as $ns | .metadata.name as $pod | .spec.volumes[]? | select(.projected != null) | .projected.sources[]? | select(.serviceAccountToken != null) | [$ns, $pod, (.serviceAccountToken.audience // "UNBOUND"), (.serviceAccountToken.expirationSeconds // "DEFAULT") | tostring] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rows showing 'UNBOUND' in the audience column indicate tokens without audience binding; specific audience strings indicate binding is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Generate a summary report of all pods with projected tokens, flagging those missing audience binding.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '[.items[] | select(.spec.volumes[]?.projected.sources[]?.serviceAccountToken != null) | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, pod: .metadata.name, audience_bound: ([ .spec.volumes[]?.projected.sources[]?.serviceAccountToken.audience ] | any(. != null))}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array where audience_bound:false identifies pods with unbound service account tokens that need remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review pod or deployment YAML manifests in source control to check for audience field presence in serviceAccountToken projected volume configurations.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -r 'serviceAccountToken' /path/to/k8s/manifests/ -A 5 | grep -E 'audience|expirationSeconds'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of 'audience:' entries confirms binding is configured; absence indicates audience-unbound tokens in those manifests.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API directly to retrieve projected volume specs for a specific pod and verify audience configuration.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumes[*].projected.sources[*].serviceAccountToken}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON output with 'audience' field present and non-empty confirms binding; output without 'audience' key confirms token_audience_binding_configured is false.

option_description: Indicates whether a projected service account token has an expiration exceeding 86400 seconds (24 hours). Tokens using the legacy automountServiceAccountToken mechanism are typically very long-lived or non-expiring. Bounded projected tokens with expirationSeconds above 86400 also qualify. Long-lived tokens increase the window of opportunity for an attacker who extracts a token from a compromised container.
security_impact: When true and `service_account_token_projected` is also true, the Rego rule `service_account_token_over_projection` fires via the condition `input.token_long_lived > 86400`. A long-lived token stolen from a container persists as a valid credential far beyond the lifetime of the workload itself, enabling sustained cross-zone authentication and privilege escalation long after the initial compromise is remediated.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Extract expirationSeconds from all projected serviceAccountToken volume sources and flag those exceeding 86400 or using legacy automount (which issues non-expiring tokens).
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | .metadata.namespace as $ns | .metadata.name as $pod | .spec.volumes[]? | select(.projected != null) | .projected.sources[]? | select(.serviceAccountToken != null) | [$ns, $pod, (.serviceAccountToken.expirationSeconds // "LEGACY_NO_EXPIRY") | tostring] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Values of 'LEGACY_NO_EXPIRY' or numeric values greater than 86400 indicate long-lived tokens; values of 3600 or lower are preferred short-lived tokens.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Decode a mounted service account token JWT to inspect its 'exp' claim and calculate actual lifetime.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl exec -n <namespace> <pod-name> -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print('exp:', d.get('exp'), 'iat:', d.get('iat'), 'lifetime_seconds:', d.get('exp',0)-d.get('iat',0))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: lifetime_seconds value above 86400 confirms token_long_lived is true; legacy tokens may show very large values or no exp claim.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Identify pods using automountServiceAccountToken without explicit projected volume configuration, which results in legacy long-lived token injection.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.automountServiceAccountToken != false) | select(([.spec.volumes[]? | select(.projected.sources[]?.serviceAccountToken != null)] | length) == 0) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, "LEGACY_AUTO_MOUNT"] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pods showing LEGACY_AUTO_MOUNT have non-expiring tokens via the legacy mechanism and should be treated as token_long_lived:true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the cluster's token expiration policy and kube-apiserver --service-account-max-token-expiration flag to understand the upper bound enforced by the API server.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver -o json | jq -r '.items[].spec.containers[].command[] | select(contains("service-account-max-token-expiration"))'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of --service-account-max-token-expiration=86400s or lower confirms a server-side cap; absence means no server-enforced maximum.

option_description: Indicates whether network flow logging is actively configured and capturing traffic on paths between trust zones within the cluster. This includes CNI-level flow logs (Cilium Hubble, Calico flow logs), iptables LOG rules applied at zone namespace boundaries, or cloud provider VPC flow logs for inter-zone node-to-node traffic.
security_impact: When false combined with `runtime_network_monitoring_solution` equal to 'none', the primary Rego trigger `unmonitored_inter_zone_traffic_paths` fires. Additionally, when false combined with `network_policy_enforcement_enabled` being false, a second trigger fires for the same exposure. Without flow logging, lateral movement between zones is invisible to defenders, allowing T1665 (Hide Infrastructure) and T1040 (Network Sniffing) techniques to go undetected and unaudited.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check whether Cilium Hubble flow logging is enabled and configured to capture inter-namespace (inter-zone) traffic.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap -n kube-system cilium-config -o jsonpath='{.data.enable-hubble}' && kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=hubble-relay --no-headers | wc -l
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output of 'true' for enable-hubble and relay pod count > 0 confirms Hubble flow logging is active; 'false' or no pods indicates it is disabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify Calico flow logging configuration by inspecting the FelixConfiguration for flow log settings.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get felixconfigurations default -o json 2>/dev/null | jq '{flowLogsEnabled: .spec.flowLogsEnabled, flowLogsFlushInterval: .spec.flowLogsFlushInterval, flowLogsCollectTcpStats: .spec.flowLogsCollectTcpStats}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: flowLogsEnabled:true with a defined flush interval confirms Calico flow logging is active between zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for iptables LOG rules applied at inter-zone VLAN or namespace boundaries on cluster nodes.
how_to_obtain.command: iptables -L -n -v | grep -i 'LOG' | grep -E 'FORWARD|zone'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: LOG rules in the FORWARD chain targeting inter-zone traffic confirm iptables-level flow logging; empty output indicates no iptables logging.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that flow log records are present and being shipped to a SIEM or log aggregator by checking for recent entries covering inter-zone traffic patterns.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=hubble-relay --tail=50 | grep -E 'flow|verdict|namespace'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Recent flow log entries with source and destination namespace fields confirms logs are being generated and captured.

option_description: Identifies the type of runtime network monitoring solution deployed to observe and record inter-zone traffic within the cluster. Values include 'none' (no monitoring), 'ebpf_based' (Cilium/Hubble, Falco with network rules, or similar eBPF tools), 'service_mesh' (Istio, Linkerd telemetry with inter-zone visibility), or 'flow_logs_only' (CNI flow logs or cloud VPC flow logs without active enforcement or deep packet inspection).
security_impact: When set to 'none', the Rego condition `input.runtime_network_monitoring_solution == 'none'` combined with `not input.inter_zone_flow_logging_enabled` triggers `unmonitored_inter_zone_traffic_paths`. When set to 'flow_logs_only' without `network_policy_enforcement_enabled`, a second trigger fires. The absence of runtime monitoring eliminates the ability to detect T1040 (Network Sniffing), T1205 (Traffic Signaling), and T1665 (Hide Infrastructure) on inter-zone paths.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Detect eBPF-based monitoring tools by checking for Cilium, Falco, or Tetragon deployments in the cluster.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.labels["k8s-app"] == "cilium" or .metadata.labels["app"] == "falco" or .metadata.labels["app"] == "tetragon" or .metadata.name | test("hubble")) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, .metadata.labels["app"] // .metadata.labels["k8s-app"]] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of cilium, falco, tetragon, or hubble pods confirms ebpf_based monitoring; absence requires checking for service mesh.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Detect service mesh telemetry deployments (Istio, Linkerd) that provide inter-zone traffic visibility.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.namespace == "istio-system" or .metadata.namespace == "linkerd" or .metadata.namespace == "linkerd-viz") | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Pods in istio-system or linkerd namespaces confirm service_mesh monitoring is deployed; check if telemetry/observability components are running.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for flow-logs-only solutions such as cloud VPC flow log configuration or CNI-only logging without a full monitoring stack.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get configmap -n kube-system -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.data | has("flowLogsEnabled") or has("flow-logs")) | [.metadata.name, (.data | to_entries[] | select(.key | test("flow|log")) | .key + "=" + .value)] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ConfigMaps with flow log entries but no eBPF or service mesh tools present indicates flow_logs_only; confirm no Cilium/Falco/Istio pods exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the platform security team to determine which runtime monitoring solution is officially deployed and whether it covers inter-zone traffic paths specifically.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written documentation naming the monitoring solution (Cilium, Falco, Istio, etc.) with configuration evidence of inter-zone traffic capture.

option_description: Indicates whether Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources or equivalent CNI-enforced policies are active on the workload or between trust zones, providing baseline ingress and egress traffic restriction. This requires both a NetworkPolicy-capable CNI plugin (Calico, Cilium, WeaveNet) and actual NetworkPolicy objects applied to the relevant namespaces.
security_impact: This attribute is referenced by two Rego rules. In `unmonitored_inter_zone_traffic_paths`, its absence triggers the exposure when flow_logs_only monitoring is present (no enforcement backing the logging) and when inter_zone_flow_logging is also absent. In `host_network_namespace_sharing`, its absence combined with host_network_enabled:true triggers a second exposure. Without NetworkPolicy enforcement, there is no baseline restriction preventing lateral movement between zones, making T1599 (Network Boundary Bridging) and T1590.003 (Network Trust Dependencies) trivially exploitable.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify that the CNI plugin supports NetworkPolicy enforcement by checking the CNI configuration and installed plugin type.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.name | test("calico|cilium|weave|canal")) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name] | @tsv' && kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '.items[0].status.conditions[] | select(.type == "Ready") | .message'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Presence of calico, cilium, or weave pods confirms NetworkPolicy-capable CNI is installed; flannel alone does NOT enforce NetworkPolicy.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all NetworkPolicy resources across namespaces to confirm policies exist and are applied to inter-zone workload namespaces.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | {namespace: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, podSelector: .spec.podSelector, ingress_rules: (.spec.ingress | length), egress_rules: (.spec.egress | length)}]'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array with NetworkPolicy objects per namespace; namespaces with zero policies have no enforcement and indicate network_policy_enforcement_enabled:false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for default-deny NetworkPolicy objects in each trust zone namespace, which is the baseline for effective enforcement.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.spec.podSelector == {} or .spec.podSelector == null) | select(.spec.ingress == null or .spec.egress == null) | [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, "DEFAULT_DENY"] | @tsv'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Namespaces with DEFAULT_DENY policies have baseline enforcement; namespaces without any matching policy have no effective restriction.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Perform a connectivity test between pods in different trust zone namespaces to empirically verify whether NetworkPolicy enforcement is blocking unauthorized inter-zone traffic.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl run test-probe --rm -it --image=busybox -n <zone-a-namespace> -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://<zone-b-service>.<zone-b-namespace>.svc.cluster.local 2>&1 | head -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connection timeout or refused indicates NetworkPolicy is enforcing zone separation; successful connection indicates enforcement is absent or misconfigured.

option_description: Controls whether a container or pod shares the host's PID namespace (seeing and signaling all host processes) or IPC namespace (accessing host shared memory segments and semaphores). When enabled, the container can interact with host-level and cross-container processes outside its isolation boundary.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers privileged_container_flag_dissolving_boundary when both privileged_mode_enabled and host_pid_or_ipc_namespace_shared are true, recognizing this combination as a compounded boundary collapse. Sharing the host PID namespace enables ptrace-based process injection (T1055.008) against host processes, cross-zone signal injection, and /proc filesystem inspection of all running workloads. Sharing the host IPC namespace exposes shared memory segments to inter-process communication attacks (T1559), allowing a compromised container to read or write data belonging to processes in higher-trust zones. The shared_pid_or_ipc_namespace_across_zones rule additionally fires when cross_zone_namespace_sharing_detected is true, escalating the finding to a direct segmentation enforcement failure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect a running Kubernetes pod spec for hostPID and hostIPC fields using kubectl with a jsonpath query.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.hostPID}{" "}{.spec.hostIPC}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns 'true true', 'true false', 'false true', or 'false false'. Any 'true' value indicates the namespace is shared with the host.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan all pods across all namespaces for hostPID or hostIPC set to true using kubectl and grep.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostPID==true or .spec.hostIPC==true) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, hostPID: .spec.hostPID, hostIPC: .spec.hostIPC}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects listing any pods with host namespace sharing enabled. Empty output indicates no violations.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Docker containers, inspect the container configuration for PidMode and IpcMode settings.
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect <container-name-or-id> --format '{{.HostConfig.PidMode}} {{.HostConfig.IpcMode}}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns 'host' for either field if the namespace is shared. Empty string or 'private' indicates proper isolation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review Kubernetes deployment or pod manifest YAML files in source control or on disk for hostPID and hostIPC declarations under the pod spec.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'hostPID\|hostIPC' /path/to/manifests/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines showing 'hostPID: true' or 'hostIPC: true' indicate misconfigured workloads. No matches means the settings are absent (defaulting to false).

typical_values: false (default, correct posture — namespaces are isolated)
true (misconfigured — seen in debug containers, node-level monitoring agents like some Prometheus node exporters, and legacy DaemonSets)

option_description: Controls whether a container or pod is attached to the host's network namespace rather than its own isolated network namespace. When enabled, the container shares the host's network interfaces, IP address, and routing table, bypassing all CNI-enforced network segmentation for that workload.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires host_network_namespace_sharing whenever host_network_enabled is true, regardless of whether network policies are present, because the container already has visibility into all host-level traffic. A secondary condition fires specifically when network_policy_enforcement_enabled is also absent, compounding the exposure. This configuration enables network sniffing of all co-located zone traffic (T1040), bridges the container directly to the host network boundary (T1599), and allows enumeration of all host system network connections (T1049).
