The finding is also weighted by workload_trust_zone — a public-facing or dmz workload with host networking represents a significantly higher blast radius than an internal workload, as it creates a direct path from external-facing traffic into the host network stack.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query a specific Kubernetes pod for the hostNetwork setting using kubectl jsonpath.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.spec.hostNetwork}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns 'true' if host network is enabled. An empty response or 'false' indicates the pod uses its own network namespace.

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all pods cluster-wide where hostNetwork is true using kubectl and jq.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.hostNetwork==true) | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, nodeName: .spec.nodeName}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON objects for each pod running with host networking. Empty output indicates no host-network pods exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Docker, inspect the NetworkMode of a running container to determine if it shares the host network stack.
how_to_obtain.command: docker inspect <container-name-or-id> --format '{{.HostConfig.NetworkMode}}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns 'host' if the container uses the host network namespace. Returns 'bridge', 'overlay', or a custom network name for properly isolated containers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Search Kubernetes manifest files and Helm chart templates for hostNetwork declarations to identify misconfigurations before deployment.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -rn 'hostNetwork:\s*true' /path/to/manifests/ /path/to/helm/charts/
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any match indicates a workload configured to use the host network namespace. Review each match to determine if it is operationally justified.

typical_values: false (default, correct posture — container uses isolated CNI-managed network namespace)
true (seen in node-level networking components such as kube-proxy, Calico node agents, and some CNI plugins; also frequently misconfigured in legacy workloads)

option_description: Classifies the security tier or trust zone of a container workload, defining its position within the network segmentation model. This classification is used to contextually score the severity of misconfigurations — the same vulnerability in a 'restricted' zone carries a higher blast radius than in an 'internal' zone — and to determine whether cross-zone namespace sharing or egress paths represent segmentation violations.
security_impact: The Rego policy references workload_trust_zone in multiple rules. The unrestricted_egress_enabling_trust_propagation rule specifically fires when workload_trust_zone is 'untrusted' or 'low' and egress policies are absent, recognizing that outbound connections from low-trust zones directly threaten trust propagation into higher zones (T1590.003, T1599). The excessive_linux_capabilities_granted, overly_permissive_ingress_between_zones, privileged_container_flag_dissolving_boundary, and host_network_namespace_sharing rules all consume this value to assess blast radius. Without a defined trust zone (value is 'unknown'), security tooling cannot correctly prioritize findings — a privileged container in a 'dmz' zone adjacent to the internet is categorically more dangerous than one in a tightly controlled 'internal' zone with no external exposure.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect Kubernetes pod and namespace labels for trust zone classification tags applied by the security or platform team.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}' && kubectl get namespace <namespace> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON map of labels. Look for keys such as 'trust-zone', 'security-tier', 'zone', or 'classification' with values matching the enum (dmz, internal, sensitive_data, public_facing, untrusted, restricted).

how_to_obtain.instruction: List all unique trust zone label values across pods cluster-wide to inventory the current classification coverage and identify unlabeled workloads.
how_to_obtain.command: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o json | jq -r '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, namespace: .metadata.namespace, zone: (.metadata.labels["trust-zone"] // "UNLABELED")} | [.namespace, .name, .zone] | @tsv' | sort -k3
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Tab-separated list of namespace, pod name, and trust zone value. Rows showing 'UNLABELED' indicate workloads that will evaluate as 'unknown' and cannot be correctly risk-scored.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the organization's network segmentation documentation, topology diagrams, and Kubernetes namespace-to-zone mapping policies maintained by the platform or security architecture team.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Request the network segmentation runbook, zone definition document, or Kubernetes namespace classification matrix from the platform engineering or security architecture team.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A document or spreadsheet mapping namespaces and workload types to trust zone classifications (dmz, internal, sensitive_data, public_facing, untrusted, restricted) with the labeling convention used in the cluster.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the Kubernetes API server directly for namespace-level zone annotations or labels that propagate trust zone classification to all workloads within that namespace.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(kubectl create token default)" https://<api-server>/api/v1/namespaces | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, labels: .metadata.labels, annotations: .metadata.annotations}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON array of namespace objects with their labels and annotations. Presence of zone classification keys confirms namespace-level trust tagging is implemented.

typical_values: unknown (default and most common — many organizations lack a formal workload classification scheme)
internal (common for backend microservices and databases not directly internet-exposed)
dmz (used for ingress controllers, API gateways, and load balancers with external-facing traffic)
public_facing (similar to dmz; applied to workloads directly serving external user requests)
sensitive_data (applied to workloads processing PII, secrets, or regulated data)
restricted (highest trust tier; applied to security tooling, vault sidecars, or compliance-scoped workloads)
untrusted (applied to user-submitted workloads, sandboxed execution environments, or third-party integrations)
